title: Design a Video Platform
summary: You'll be able to design a YouTube-style platform end to end: resumable uploads, a parallel transcoding pipeline, adaptive bitrate streaming, CDN delivery, and the storage and bandwidth math behind it.

questions.prompt: What is **adaptive bitrate streaming**, and why does it require cutting each rendition into short segments?
questions.hint: What happens to a viewer whose connection drops from 8 Mbps to 1 Mbps halfway through a video?
keyPoints: The video is encoded into several renditions (resolutions/bitrates) listed in a manifest (HLS .m3u8 or DASH .mpd)
The player measures throughput and buffer level and picks the rendition it can sustain
Each rendition is split into short segments (typically 2–6 s) aligned at the same time points across renditions
Alignment lets the player switch quality at any segment boundary instead of restarting a single large file
The goal is to avoid rebuffering (stalls) while using the best quality the connection allows

questions.prompt:
A platform receives **50,000 hours** of uploaded video per day. Each video is transcoded into renditions at **0.5, 1, 2.5 and 4.5 Mbps**. Originals are also kept, averaging **6 Mbps**.

How much new storage is needed per day and per year, before any replication or erasure-coding overhead?
questions.hint: Add the ladder first, multiply by 3,600 seconds, and divide by 8 for bytes.
keyPoints: Ladder total = 0.5 + 1 + 2.5 + 4.5 = 8.5 Mbps
One hour of all renditions = 8.5 Mbps × 3,600 s / 8 = 3,825 MB ≈ 3.8 GB; one hour of original = 6 × 3,600 / 8 = 2.7 GB
Per hour of video ≈ 6.5 GB total; × 50,000 h ≈ 326 TB/day
Per year ≈ 326 TB × 365 ≈ 119 PB (≈ 120 PB)
Correctly converts bits to bytes (divide by 8)
questions.answer:
```text
Renditions: 8.5 Mbps × 3,600 s = 30,600 Mb = 3,825 MB per hour
Original:   6 Mbps × 3,600 s   = 21,600 Mb = 2,700 MB per hour
Total per hour of video        ≈ 6,525 MB ≈ 6.5 GB
Per day:  50,000 × 6.525 GB    ≈ 326 TB
Per year: 326 TB × 365         ≈ 119 PB
```

questions.prompt:
At peak, **4 million** people are watching at once, at an average of **3 Mbps** each. Your CDN has a **97%** byte hit rate.

(a) What is total egress to viewers? (b) What bandwidth must the origin serve? (c) If the hit rate drops to 90% during a launch of many new videos, how much does origin load grow?
questions.hint: Origin traffic is only the misses: (1 − hit rate) × total.
keyPoints: Total egress = 4M × 3 Mbps = 12,000,000 Mbps = 12 Tbps
Origin load at 97% = 3% × 12 Tbps = 0.36 Tbps = 360 Gbps
Origin load at 90% = 10% × 12 Tbps = 1.2 Tbps
Going from 97% to 90% hit rate more than triples origin load (×3.3), showing why miss rate, not hit rate, is what to watch
Mentions mitigations such as an origin shield or pre-warming caches
questions.answer:
```text
(a) 4,000,000 × 3 Mbps = 12 Tbps
(b) 0.03 × 12 Tbps = 360 Gbps from origin
(c) 0.10 × 12 Tbps = 1.2 Tbps → 1.2 / 0.36 ≈ 3.3× more origin load
```

questions.prompt: Design the path from "creator taps Upload on a phone" to "video is playable". Include how you handle a **dropped connection during upload** and a **transcoding worker that crashes halfway through**.
questions.hint: Bytes should never touch your API servers. Think queue visibility timeouts for the worker.
keyPoints: API creates the video record (status uploading) and returns presigned multipart upload URLs for object storage
The client uploads parts independently and retries/resumes only missing parts; a complete call assembles them
Completion publishes an event to a queue; status becomes processing
An orchestrator splits the video into keyframe-aligned chunks and fans out chunk × rendition encode tasks to workers, then packages segments and manifests
A crashed worker never acks its task, so the queue redelivers it after a visibility timeout; tasks are idempotent (deterministic output keys)
When all tasks finish, status becomes ready and the manifest URL is served via the CDN

questions.prompt: Write `pickRendition(renditions, measuredKbps, bufferSeconds)` that returns the highest-bitrate rendition whose bitrate is at most **80%** of measured throughput, or at most **50%** when the buffer holds less than 10 seconds. If none fit, return the lowest rendition. Each rendition looks like `{ name: "720p", kbps: 2500 }` and the array is not sorted.
questions.hint: Compute a budget, sort by kbps descending, and return the first that fits.
keyPoints: Computes budget = measuredKbps × 0.8, or × 0.5 when bufferSeconds < 10
Does not assume the input is sorted (sorts a copy or scans for the max that fits)
Returns the highest rendition with kbps <= budget
Falls back to the lowest-bitrate rendition when nothing fits
Does not mutate the input array

questions.prompt: Finance shows that **70% of uploaded videos get fewer than 100 views ever**, yet you transcode every upload into 6 renditions including AV1, and store everything on hot storage with 3 replicas. Propose changes that cut cost substantially without hurting popular videos.
questions.hint: Pay for quality only when a video earns it, and remember the storage options from Day 36.
keyPoints: Transcode new uploads into a small default ladder (e.g. 360p/720p in H.264) and add more renditions or AV1 only when views cross a threshold
Optionally transcode rare renditions on demand (just-in-time) for cold videos, accepting a slower first view
Move segments of cold/old videos to cheaper storage classes (lifecycle rules), keeping hot videos on fast storage
Replace 3× replication with erasure coding (~1.4–1.5× overhead) for durable cold storage
Quantifies the effect (e.g. 70% of videos with ~1/3 of the renditions and half the storage overhead) and mentions monitoring popularity to promote videos
